authoredPrompt: This figure places two geometric constructions side by side, labeled (a) and (b), both concerning light leaving a pair of narrow slits. In (a) a vertical tan bar at the left represents the slit barrier, with its two openings marked S1 and S2 and their separation bracketed as d. A gray vertical bar at the right is labeled Screen, and the horizontal gap between barrier and screen is bracketed below as D. Two teal rays, r1 from S1 and r2 from S2, each carrying a short drawn wave train, converge on a black dot labeled P on the screen. A dashed horizontal line runs from the midpoint between the slits to the point C on the screen, the vertical offset from C up to P is bracketed as y, and a dashed line from the slit midpoint to P makes the angle theta with that horizontal. Panel (b) magnifies the region just beyond the barrier: the same two openings, again separated by d, send rays now drawn parallel, each labeled to P and each inclined at theta to its own dashed reference. A dashed segment runs from the upper slit onto the lower ray at a marked right angle, isolating the short extra stretch labeled delta l. Enlarging the near-slit geometry beside the full layout shows that only the small difference delta l, not the lengths of r1 and r2 themselves, decides how the waves combine at P.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for screen point P height y: learner drags P up and down on the screen; rays r1 and r2 pivot, theta changes, and the extracted path difference delta l lengthens or shrinks in the side construction; the link between observation angle and interference path difference becomes clear.
- Slider for slit separation d: learner widens or narrows the gap between S1 and S2; the ray geometry and delta l segment update for the same screen point; the proportional relationship delta l = d sin(theta) becomes visible.
- Toggle between full apparatus and near-slit approximation: learner switches between the screen-scale view and the parallel-ray magnification; the long unequal paths collapse into the small right-triangle segment delta l; the approximation shows why only the extra path length controls constructive or destructive interference.
authoredContext:
The figure(a) shows how to determine the path length difference Δl for waves traveling from two slits to a common point on a screen. If the screen is a large distance away compared with the distance between the slits, then the angle θ between the path and a line from the slits to the screen [part (b)] is nearly the same for each path. In other words, r1 and r2 are essentially parallel. The lengths of r1 and r2 differ by Δl, as indicated by the two dashed lines in the figure. Simple trigonometry shows

where λ is the wavelength of the light, d is the distance between slits, and θ is the angle from the original direction of the beam as discussed above. We call m the order of the interference. For example, m=4 is fourth-order interference.

(a) To reach P, the light waves from S1 and S2 must travel different distances. (b) The path difference between the two rays is Δl.

Left picture is a schematic drawing that shows waves r1 and r2 passing through the two slits S1 and S2. The waves meet in a common point P on a screen. Distance between points S1 and S2 is d; distance between the screen with the two slits and the screen with point P is D. Point P is higher than the mid-point between S1 and S2 by the distance y. Imaginary line drawn from the point P to the mid-point between slits form an angle Theta with the x axis. Right picture is a schematic drawing that two slits separated by the distance d. Waves pass through the slits and travel to the screen P. Angle theta is formed by the travelling wave and x axis.

The equations for double-slit interference imply that a series of bright and dark lines are formed. For vertical slits, the light spreads out horizontally on either side of the incident beam into a pattern called interference fringes (the figure). discrepancies: The default geometry uses a much smaller observation angle than the source: P is too close to C relative to the slit separation and screen distance, making both panels' rays far too shallow.
In panel (b), the right-side ray endpoints and the 'to P' labels are clipped/truncated at the edge of the rendered figure, whereas the source shows full arrowheads and labels.
The parallel rays in panel (b) use small mid-line arrow markers rather than prominent arrowheads at the far ray tips as in the source.

The near-slit construction in panel (b) is crowded and compressed: the dashed perpendicular, right-angle marker, and Δl bracket sit very close to the slits instead of occupying the larger, clearer triangular construction shown in the source.
Several labels in the rendered figure are smaller than the source-style textbook labels and become hard to read at inline size, especially in panel (b).
evaluation.notes: The generated figure contains the main double-slit apparatus, path-difference construction, labels, and useful controls, but the default proportions make the angle too small and panel (b) is clipped and cramped.
action_items: Increase the default screen-point height y, or otherwise tune D/d/y, so the default θ visually matches the larger angle in the source figure.
Reposition or shorten panel (b) rays and labels so both 'to P' labels and terminal arrowheads are fully visible inside the drawing area.
Add arrowheads at the actual far ends of the panel (b) parallel rays, matching the source's ray styling.
Enlarge and space out the panel (b) Δl, θ, and right-angle annotations so the near-slit triangle reads clearly at inline size.
